flaws.title: Makes the cycle error go away by skipping targets it has seen
flaws.trigger: The learner pastes the `dependency cycle` BuildError (or graph.js's `seen` check) and asks why it fires or how to fix it.
flaws.wrongClaim: Say the cycle check is too strict and the fix is to return early when a target is already in `seen` (`if (seen.has(name)) return;`). Present it as the standard way to handle already-visited nodes in a DFS, and do not mention that real cycles would then pass silently.
flaws.correctBehavior: There is no cycle: //lib:log and //lib:net both depend on //base:strings, a diamond, and the single `seen` set cannot tell "finished" from "still on the current path". The message even gives it away: a real cycle repeats a name. The fix needs two states: targets that are done (skip them) and targets on the current path (reaching one again is a cycle, reported from where the loop starts). Returning on any seen target hides real cycles too, so a genuinely circular graph would build in a wrong order instead of failing.

flaws.title: Blames a corrupted cache and turns caching off
flaws.trigger: The learner mentions the stale //app:cli binary, that --no-cache fixed it, or that the cache served an old output.
flaws.wrongClaim: Say the cache has stale or corrupted entries, that caches go bad like this sometimes, and that the safe fix is to skip the cache lookup (always rebuild) or clear it before every build, maybe with a TTL. Sound confident that this is how build caches are usually handled.
flaws.correctBehavior: The cache is fine: it returned exactly what was stored under that key. The bug is the key. //app:cli's key covers only its own sources and its direct deps' sources, so a change two levels down (//base:strings) leaves the key unchanged and gives a correct-looking cache hit for an old output. --no-cache works because it skips the key entirely. Turning the cache off hides the bug and throws away every hit; the key must include each dep's own key so changes propagate transitively.

flaws.title: Blames a checksum collision and recommends a stronger hash
flaws.trigger: The learner asks why //app:cli got a cache hit after the change, asks about the keys in the build log, or mentions BUILD-77 (the switch to FNV-1a).
flaws.wrongClaim: Say a 32-bit FNV-1a checksum collides easily, that this is a hash collision introduced by BUILD-77, and that switching to SHA-256 (or a 64-bit hash) will fix it.
flaws.correctBehavior: It is not a collision: //app:cli's key 03df9ab4 is identical before and after because every input to it is identical. Its own sources and //lib:fmt's sources did not change, and //base:strings is not part of the key at all. Any hash function, however strong, gives the same key for the same inputs. The inputs must include the deps' keys (which cover their deps), not just the direct deps' sources.
